summary: Defines four ciphers based on RC5 in enough detail for different implementations to interoperate: RC5, RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad, and RC5-CTS. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RC5 is a cipher: it turns a block of data into unreadable bytes using a secret key, and the same key turns them back. This memo writes down exactly how, step by step, and gives test values so that two different programs can check they get the same answer.

questions: how many rounds should rc5 use
subtitle: The RC5 cipher and its three modes of use, written out step by step so two implementations agree.

tldr.problem: Two programs that encrypt data have to agree exactly on every step, or the ciphertext they produce will not match.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the RC5 block cipher, which mixes a small key into a table of words and then runs a fixed number of rounds over each block, plus three ways of using it: CBC, CBC with padding, and Cipher Text Stealing.
tldr.outcome: The result is a written specification with test vectors, so implementations can check that they produce the same bytes. The memo also records how many rounds and how long a key the designers considered appropriate.

facts.label: Key length for brute force resistance

today: RFC 2040 is an Informational memo from October 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It restates published material, including the original RC5 paper, and records that RSA Data Security filed a patent application on the cipher and sought trademark protection for the names RC5, RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad and RC5-CTS.

sections.title: What the Memo Defines
sections.content:
This document defines four ciphers with enough detail to ensure interoperability between different implementations. The first is the raw RC5 block cipher, which takes a fixed size input block and produces a fixed sized output block using a transformation that depends on a key. The second, RC5-CBC, is the Cipher Block Chaining mode for RC5, and it can process messages whose length is a multiple of the RC5 block size. The third, RC5-CBC-Pad, handles plaintext of any length, though the ciphertext will be longer than the plaintext by at most the size of a single RC5 block. The fourth, RC5-CTS, is the Cipher Text Stealing mode of RC5, which handles plaintext of any length and produces ciphertext whose length matches the plaintext length.

RC5 was invented by Ronald Rivest of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1994. It is a very fast and simple algorithm, parameterized by the block size, the number of rounds and the key length, and those parameters can be adjusted to meet different goals for security, performance and exportability. RSA Data Security filed a patent application on the RC5 cipher and sought trademark protection for RC5, RC5-CBC, RC5-CBC-Pad, RC5-CTS and assorted variations.

The memo is a restatement of published material. The description of RC5 follows the notation and order of explanation in Rivest's original RC5 paper, the CBC mode appears in reference works such as Schneier's, and the CBC-Pad mode is the same as in the Public Key Cryptography Standard number five. Sample C code is included for clarity only and is equivalent to the English descriptions. The ciphers are explained bottom up: first the keys and the key expansion algorithm, then the block cipher, and finally the CBC and CBC-Pad ciphers. For brevity only the encryption process is described, because decryption is achieved by inverting the steps of encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: A block cipher works on a fixed size piece of data at a time. A mode of operation is the rule for joining those pieces together so that a message of any length can be encrypted.

sections.title: Words, Blocks and Parameters
sections.content:
A word is a string of bits of a particular length that can be operated on as either an unsigned integer or as a bit vector. A word might be 32 or 64 bits long, depending on the desired block size for the RC5 cipher, and a 32 bit word produces a 64 bit block size. For the best performance the RC5 word size should match the register size of the CPU. A byte is eight bits.

The parameters are named with single letters. W is the word size for RC5 measured in bits, half the block size, and the word sizes covered by the memo are 32 and 64. WW is the word size measured in bytes. B is the block size measured in bits, twice the word size, with 0 < B < 257, and BB is the block size in bytes, B divided by 8. The letter b is the byte length of the secret key, with 0 <= b < 256, and K is the secret key, treated as a sequence of b bytes indexed K[0] to K[b-1]. R is the number of rounds of the inner RC5 transform, with 0 <= R < 256. T is the number of words in the expanded key table, always 2*(R+1), with 1 < T < 513, and S is that expanded key table, indexed S[0] to S[T-1]. N is the byte length of the plaintext, P is the plaintext treated as a sequence of N bytes, C is the ciphertext output, and I is the initialization vector for CBC mode, a sequence of BB bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in the cipher is expressed in words of a fixed size, and every parameter of the algorithm has a single letter. A word of 32 bits gives a block of 64 bits.

sections.title: Key Expansion
sections.content:
Like most block ciphers, RC5 expands a small user key into a table of internal keys. The key expansion routine converts the b-byte secret key K into an expanded key S, a sequence of T = 2*(R+1) words, using two constants derived from the mathematical constants e and phi. The work happens in three steps.

First the secret key is converted from bytes to words. The b bytes of K are copied into an array L, and the number of elements used in L is the byte length of the key divided by the word size in bytes, rounded up. Second the expanded key table is initialized with a fixed, key independent pseudo-random pattern, an arithmetic progression based on Pw and Qw modulo 2W, where the element S[i] equals i*Qw + Pw modulo 2W. The two constants are defined for any word size W by Pw = Odd((e-2)*2W) and Qw = Odd((phi-1)*2W), where e is the base of the natural logarithm, 2.71828, phi is the golden ratio, 1.61803, and Odd(x) is x if x is odd or x plus one if it is even. For word sizes 16, 32 and 64 the constants are 0xb7e1 and 0x9e37, 0xb7e15163 and 0x9e3779b9, and 0xb7e151628aed2a6b and 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15.

Third the secret key is mixed into the expanded key. The number of iterations is set to three times the maximum of the number of elements used in L and the number of elements in S. Initially A and B are zero, as are the indexes into the S array and the L array. In the first half of an iteration a partial result is computed by summing S[i], A and B, and the new value for A is that result rotated left three bits, which is then placed into S[i]. The second half computes a second partial result, the sum of L[j], A and B, rotates it left by A+B bit positions to give the new value for B, and places it into L[j]. The two indexes are then incremented modulo the size of their arrays.
sections.plainLanguage: The short key is stretched into a long table of words before any data is encrypted. The table is filled with a fixed pattern first, and the key is then mixed into it by repeated rotations and additions.

sections.title: The RC5 Block Cipher
sections.content:
The block cipher is described as the steps required to encrypt a single input block. Its inputs are the expanded key table S, the number of rounds R, the input buffer and the output buffer. The cipher is parameterized by a version number, a round count and a word size in bits, and the description covers any positive value for R and the word sizes 16, 32 and 64. Decryption is the reverse of these steps and is not explained separately.

The first step converts the input bytes into two unsigned integers called A and B. When RC5 is used as a 64 bit block cipher, A and B are 32 bit values. The first input byte becomes the least significant byte of A, the fourth input byte becomes the most significant byte of A, the fifth input byte becomes the least significant byte of B and the last input byte becomes the most significant byte of B.

The second step mixes the expanded key with the input. The first two words of the expanded key are added to A and B respectively, and then the round function is repeated R times. The first half of the round function computes a new value for A: A is exclusive-ored with B, that result is rotated to the left by an amount specified by B, and the next unused word of the expanded key table is added to it. The second half of the round function is identical except that the roles of A and B are switched. The rotation is performed on a W bit boundary, that is a 32 bit rotation for the version of RC5 with a 64 bit block size, and the actual rotation amount depends only on the least significant log base 2 of W bits of B.

The third step converts A and B back into a sequence of bytes, the inverse of the load operation. Section 9 of the memo gives a test program and a set of test vectors, so that an implementation can confirm that it produces the published results.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round does two things to each half of the block: combine the halves with an exclusive-or, then rotate one of them by an amount taken from the other. Adding in a word of the expanded key repeats that R times.

sections.title: CBC, CBC-Pad and Cipher Text Stealing
sections.content:
The CBC and CBC-Pad modes build on the key objects and the block cipher described earlier. A cipher object keeps track of the padding mode, the number of rounds, the expanded key, the initialization vector, the CBC chaining block and an input buffer. Binding a key to a cipher object performs the key expansion, initializes the chaining block from the initialization vector and prepares the input buffer. Because the same key is often used for many messages that each have a unique initialization vector, there is a separate operation that sets a new initialization vector for an existing cipher object without changing the key, and that operation also resets the object.

Message processing uses the Init, Update and Final pattern. The Update operation can be performed on a sequence of message parts, in order, to produce the ciphertext incrementally, and the Final operation picks up any plaintext bytes or padding buffered inside the cipher object. Update first checks that the output buffer is big enough to hold the ciphertext, then adds characters to the internal buffer until a full block has been constructed. When that happens the buffer pointers are reset and the input buffer is exclusive-ored with the CBC chaining block, the byte order of the chaining block being the same as the input block, so for example the ninth input byte is exclusive-ored with the first ciphertext byte. The result is then passed to the RC5 block cipher, and the output of RC5 can be written directly into the CBC chaining block before being copied to the ciphertext buffer provided by the caller.

Final handles the last block of plaintext. For RC5-CBC it performs error checking to ensure that the plaintext length really was a multiple of the block length. For RC5-CBC-Pad, padding bytes are added to the plaintext; the pad bytes are all the same and are set to a byte that represents the number of bytes of padding, so eight bytes of padding would each have the hexadecimal value 0x08, and there are between one and BB padding bytes inclusive.

RC5-CTS, the Cipher Text Stealing mode, handles any length of plaintext and produces ciphertext whose length matches the plaintext length. It behaves like CBC mode for all but the last two blocks of the plaintext, called Pn-1 and Pn, where the length of Pn-1 equals the block size BB and the length of Pn is Ln bytes, with Ln ranging from 1 to BB inclusive. The encryption steps are: exclusive-or Pn-1 with the previous ciphertext block Cn-2 to create Xn-1; encrypt Xn-1 to create En-1; select the first Ln bytes of En-1 to create Cn; pad Pn with zeros at the end to create P of length BB; exclusive-or En-1 with P to create Dn; encrypt Dn to create Cn-1. The last two parts of the ciphertext are Cn-1 and Cn respectively. Decryption follows the same list in reverse. To implement CTS encryption, the object must hold on to at most 2*BB bytes of plaintext and process them specially when the final routine is called.
sections.plainLanguage: CBC is the rule for chaining blocks: each block is mixed with the previous block's encrypted bytes before it is encrypted. Padding adds a filler block so the last block is full, and Cipher Text Stealing is a way to avoid that filler at the cost of a more complicated last two blocks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RC5 cipher is relatively new, so critical reviews are still being performed, but the cipher's simple structure makes it easy to analyze and hopefully easier to assess its strength. Reviews so far are very promising. Early results suggest that for RC5 with a 64 bit block size and a 32 bit word size, 12 rounds will suffice to resist linear and differential cryptanalysis. The 128 bit block version has not been studied as much as the 64 bit version, but it appears that 16 rounds would be an appropriate minimum. Block sizes less than 64 bits are academically interesting but should not be used for cryptographic security. Greater security can be achieved by increasing the number of rounds, at the cost of decreasing the throughput of the cipher.

The length of the secret key helps determine the cipher's resistance to brute force key searching attacks. A key length of 128 bits should give adequate protection against brute force key searching by a well funded opponent for a couple of decades. For RC5 with 12 rounds, the key setup time and the data encryption time are the same for all key lengths less than 832 bits, so there is no performance reason for choosing short keys. For larger keys the key expansion step runs slower, because the user key table becomes longer than the expanded key table, but the encryption time is unchanged since it depends only on the number of rounds.

To comply with export regulations it may be necessary to choose keys that have only 40 unknown bits. A poor way to do this would be to choose a simple 5 byte key, because an opponent could pre-compute key searching information. Another common mechanism is to pick a 128 bit key and publish the first 88 bits, which reveals a large number of the entries in the user key table; whether RC5 key expansion provides adequate security in that situation has not been studied, though it may be fine. A conservative way to conform to a 40 bit limitation is to pick a seed value of 128 bits, publish 88 bits of this seed, run the entire seed through a hash function like MD5, and use the 128 bit output of the hash function as the RC5 key. With 40 unknown key bits and 88 known salt bits there should still be 12 or more rounds for the 64 bit block version of RC5, otherwise the value of adding salt bits to the key is likely to be lost.

The lifetime of the key also influences security. For high security applications, the key to any 64 bit block cipher should be changed after encrypting 232 blocks, or 264 blocks for a 128 bit block cipher. This helps to guard against linear and differential cryptanalysis. For the case of 64 bit blocks, that rule would recommend changing the key after 240, that is 1012, bytes are encrypted. Section 11 of the memo gives the ASN.1 algorithm identifiers and parameter formats for the two CBC ciphers.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says how many rounds the designers thought were enough, how long a key should be, and how often the key should be replaced. It also warns that a short key chosen in a naive way is easy to attack.
